reception.text: Locally the designation drew little fight, since the tower sat on federal land no one was contesting.

In the 1906 campaign Cheyenne's Democratic paper charged that Wyoming's Republican congressman, Frank Mondell, had opposed Roosevelt on every major measure and kept up his opposition after Congress adjourned; the Mondell-backing Wyoming Tribune answered four days later.
reception.source: Cheyenne Daily Leader, October 20, 1906, p. 4; Wyoming Tribune, October 24, 1906, p. 4

political_impact.text: Mondell had already protested the late-July 1906 withdrawal of 109 Wyoming townships, more than two and a half million acres by his count, as coal land, at least ten days before the Devils Tower proclamation.
political_impact.source: Laramie Republican, September 14, 1906, p. 2; Sheridan Post, September 21, 1906

political_impact.text: As the first use of the Antiquities Act, and for a natural wonder rather than a ruin, it signaled the broad reading of the law that would soon carry the Grand Canyon.

legacy.text: Devils Tower remains the founding unit of the national monument system, and the power first used here has been used by presidents of both parties ever since.
The tower is still sacred to many tribes; the National Park Service names the Arapaho, Crow, Cheyenne, Shoshone and Lakota among more than twenty.

Under the 1995 Climbing Management Plan the Park Service asks visitors to voluntarily refrain from climbing on the tower or scrambling inside the Tower Trail loop throughout June, a request it reports has sharply reduced June climbing.
legacy.source: National Park Service, Climbing Management Plan (February 1995; 2006 update)

today.name: Devils Tower National Monument
today.note: Now 1,347 acres, about 194 more than the 1,152.91 reserved in 1906.

related.note: Grand Canyon National Monument carried the same broad reading of the Antiquities Act.

later_actions.text: The National Park Service adopted a Climbing Management Plan with a voluntary June closure, worked out with climbers and American Indian representatives.
The Interior Secretary withdrew the plan's June ban on commercial guiding after a court had preliminarily enjoined it in June 1996.
The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of climbers' challenge to the voluntary June closure, holding they lacked standing.
later_actions.source: Bear Lodge Multiple Use Association v. Babbitt, 175 F.3d 814 (10th Cir. 1999)

later_actions.text: The Supreme Court declined to review the Bear Lodge case.
